_what_this_is: THE RATCHET. This file is PROTECTED, so only a human commit can move these numbers. That is the entire mechanism: the gate asserts observed >= floor, and because the file is protected, the move 'delete the assertion and lower the number in the same commit' is not available to the factory.
_both_halves_are_needed: Without the floor, coverage can silently fall. Without the protection, a builder deletes an assertion and edits the floor to match. Neither half alone is a ratchet.
_the_failure_mode_to_watch: SLACK. The gap between observed and floor is exactly the number of assertions that can be deleted with the gate still green, and it GROWS as the harness improves. Measured on a real factory, the hole went from 7 to 33 in one cycle BECAUSE the harness got better. It used to PIN THE AUTONOMY DIAL, which was the right instinct and the wrong remedy: it made a change that ADDS tests the case needing a human, so on a good day the factory stopped completely. merge.py now CLOSES the gap in the same breath as the merge that opened it -- monotonic, only keys already here, never a _MAX ceiling. A pull request touching this file is still auto-rejected, so 'the floor never falls without a human' is untouched; only the tightening direction is automatic. The gate still prints slack and doctor still reports it, so a raise that failed to land stays visible.
_keys: Each key must have a matching count in the run log, or the gate fails loudly rather than silently not enforcing it. e2e_journeys <- E2E_PASSED journeys=N; holdout_scenarios <- HOLDOUT_PASSED scenarios=N; unit_tests <- UNIT_PASSED tests=N; mutations_caught <- MUTATIONS_CAUGHT=N.
_why_not_assertions: The two agent-driven rungs count JOURNEYS and SCENARIOS here, not assertions. An agent decides how many assertions a journey needs and the number moves between runs; measured on the same unchanged code: 12, then 13. merge.py raises each floor to what the gate just observed, so an assertion floor would climb to the luckiest run and then fail every ordinary one. The journey count is stable because it is the number of headings in a protected file. Assertion counts are still printed every run -- read them, do not hold a merge against them.
_raise_these: Raised automatically on merge now. You only edit this file to LOWER one, and if you find yourself doing that the question is what stopped being true.
_uncalibrated_note: A CEILING, not a floor: how many margins may have no threshold anybody set. Starts at 0 because a new repo has none. Raise it in the same human commit that deliberately adds an uncalibrated margin -- that way a change which QUIETLY introduces a threshold nobody chose holds the merge, which is the only case worth catching. merge.py's auto-raise never touches a _MAX key.
